nameStory: The 'Minute' Aeolis gets its name from being truly tiny - among the smallest sea slugs you'll find in New England waters. The word 'aeolis' refers to the finger-like projections (called cerata) on its back that wave like sea anemone tentacles, named after Aeolus, the Greek god of wind.
description: The Minute Aeolis is a tiny sea slug that looks like a miniature underwater caterpillar with finger-like projections sprouting from its back. These translucent creatures are typically less than half an inch long and belong to a group called nudibranchs - sea slugs that breathe through external gills. Their soft, jelly-like bodies glide along surfaces using a muscular foot, and they're part of the fascinating world of marine gastropods (snails without shells).

idTips.label: Finger-like projections
idTips.description: Multiple thin, finger-like cerata extend from the back like tiny translucent fingers, often with colorful tips that may appear orange or reddish

idTips.label: Tiny size
idTips.description: Extremely small, typically measuring less than half an inch long - you'll need to look closely to spot these miniature sea slugs

idTips.label: Translucent body
idTips.description: Body appears semi-transparent and jelly-like with a pale, whitish or yellowish coloration that lets you see internal structures

idTips.label: Smooth gliding movement
idTips.description: Moves with a characteristic smooth, flowing motion across surfaces using its muscular foot, leaving no visible trail

idTips.label: Two tentacles
idTips.description: Has two sensory tentacles (rhinophores) at the front of its head that help it navigate and find food

habitat: Look for Minute Aeolis in shallow marine waters along rocky shores, tide pools, and on dock pilings throughout New England's coast. They're often found crawling on hydroids (tiny colonial animals that look like fuzzy growths on rocks and seaweed) which serve as their primary food source.

seasonality.spring: Active as waters warm, beginning to appear in shallow areas and tide pools where they feed on emerging hydroid colonies.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most easily spotted in warm tide pools and shallow coastal waters during low tide exploration.
seasonality.fall: Still active in early fall but may move to slightly deeper waters as temperatures begin to cool.
seasonality.winter: Much less active and harder to find, likely moving to deeper waters or becoming dormant in protected crevices.

funFact: Despite being smaller than your fingernail, the Minute Aeolis is a specialized predator that can steal the stinging cells from the hydroids it eats and transfer them to the tips of its finger-like projections, turning itself into a tiny armed fortress!
confusionNotes: Can be confused with other small nudibranchs, but the combination of extremely small size and distinctive finger-like cerata helps distinguish it. Remember: if it's tiny, translucent, and has multiple finger-like projections, you've likely found a Minute Aeolis.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'nudibranch' literally means 'naked gills' - these sea slugs evolved from shelled snails but lost their shells over time, developing external breathing structures instead. Don't be confused by the scientific name 'Eubranchus' which means 'good gills' - it refers to their well-developed cerata.
compareHints: The Minute Aeolis is much smaller than its relative the club-gilled nudibranch (Eubranchus pallidus), which grows larger and has more club-shaped rather than finger-like cerata. Eubranchus scintillans tends to have more sparkling or iridescent qualities, while the Minute Aeolis appears more simply translucent with colored tips on its projections.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its relatives like the minute aeolis, the club-gilled nudibranch has more distinctly club-shaped cerata rather than pointed ones.
The sparkling nudibranch differs from its relatives by having distinctly club-shaped rhinophores and cerata arranged in tight clusters rather than rows.
